issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
issues.explanation: For a 42-year-old married male ship captain with a man-made disaster trauma, 'sexual situations or intimacy' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the disaster had a sexual/interpersonal component, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other trigger items (object throwing, uniforms) fit danger/aggression themes, making this item stand out as clinically incongruent with the trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: 'Sexual coping' appears to be organized around the same sexualized theme as the sexual trigger, but that theme is otherwise absent from Threat, Negative Appraisals, and the disaster trauma context. In this profile it does not cohere with the dominant formulation of external danger, mistrust, and vigilance, whereas dropping responsibilities and gambling are more plausibly linked to avoidance/arousal management.

vignette:
David is a 42-year-old ship captain who came to treatment after more than a year of trying to manage on his own what he still calls "that blast." He is married and had spent most of his adult life feeling steady at sea, used to responsibility and to making decisions that affected other people's safety. The event that now dominates his inner life took place during a man-made disaster aboard a commercial vessel moving through a busy port corridor. In his account, the danger arrived with shocking force and human culpability. There was a sudden explosion on board, a violent bang that seemed to tear through the metal around him, followed by shouting, objects being hurled by the force of the blast, and loose equipment skidding and crashing across the deck. He remembers seeing one crewman's gear thrown sideways and hearing another man yell for instructions. In the confusion that followed, emergency responders came in uniforms that he now notices instantly anywhere he goes. What has stayed with him most sharply is not only the sound and impact, but the conviction that this happened because someone's decisions were reckless and that the people responsible have never truly been held to account.

In the weeks afterward, David tried to return to his routines as if discipline would settle him. Instead, ordinary moments began to acquire the feeling of threat. A slammed container door, construction noise on the docks, even a muffled bang from equipment could stop him cold, his body reacting before he had time to think. Seeing police or military uniforms in the port, at gas stations, or outside public buildings pulled him back to the responders and the immediate aftermath of the explosion. Object throwing became especially difficult to tolerate. If a deckhand tossed a line too sharply, if someone at home threw keys onto the counter, or if he saw a stranger angrily fling something in a parking lot, David felt a jolt of alarm that made the scene seem suddenly dangerous.

Over time, his world narrowed in practical ways. He had come to believe that he could not rely on other people, a view that had settled into his work as much as his home life. On the ship he checked crew members repeatedly, watched faces for signs of recklessness or volatility, and scanned constantly for the kind of person who might cause harm. He was vigilant around unfamiliar workers in the port and in any new setting where he could not quickly judge who was safe. He began turning down certain duties and delegating or altogether dropping responsibilities he would once have taken on without hesitation, especially tasks that meant entering unfamiliar facilities or crowded operational areas. This had consequences for his standing at work; colleagues noticed that he was no longer willing to go ashore for some meetings or inspections, and his wife noticed how much effort it took him to leave the predictable spaces he felt he could control.

His need to assess danger shaped even small decisions. In restaurants during shore leave, David insisted on the seat with the clearest line to the door and the fewest people behind him. In waiting rooms, he sat at the edge rather than in the center, visibly tense until he had mapped the room. Unfamiliar places felt intolerable because, as he put it, he could not assess the danger fast enough. Nights became their own battleground. He had difficulty falling asleep because some part of him remained convinced he needed to stay alert. He lay awake listening for sounds in the house or replaying whether doors were locked, telling himself that letting his guard down would be irresponsible.

At the same time, he avoided his own thoughts with determination. David said that if he let himself think too directly about the explosion, he would not be able to handle what came up. When images or fragments pressed in, he pushed them away by keeping busy, walking the decks, checking things twice, or, increasingly, gambling. What began as occasional time at casinos during port calls or online betting at home became a regular way to distract himself and produce a different kind of adrenaline, something he could enter on purpose rather than have forced on him. His wife knew about the money they had lost before she understood why he kept returning to it.

What finally brought David to seek help was a convergence of strain at home and work. After freezing during a loud bang on the docks and later refusing an assignment in an unfamiliar port area, he saw that his attempts to manage were altering the way he captained and the way he lived with his family. He arrived for treatment guarded, choosing his chair carefully and watching the hallway when anyone passed in uniform outside the clinic window. He was adamant that the people responsible had never faced consequences, and there was bitterness in the way he said it. What frightened him most was the possibility that if he stopped staying alert, something catastrophic would happen again, or that if he let himself fully think about the disaster, he would come apart. At the same time, he said he was tired of living as if every bang, every stranger, and every room had to be survived.
